before:
I am that Merlin of whom the legends tell
that the devil was my father — a lie
that time has only made more believable.
Prince of magic, monarch and treasurer
of the lore of Zoroaster, I watch with a jealous eye
as the present age tries to bury
the gallant deeds of bold knights-errant,
who are, and always have been, dear to my heart.
Enchanters, magicians, and their kind
are mostly hard of heart; I am not.
Mine is a tender heart, soft and compassionate,
and its delight is to do good to everyone.
In the dim caverns of gloomy Dis,
where my soul now dwells, tracing
mystic lines and characters, there reached me
the sorrow-laden cry of the fair one,
the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso.
I knew of her enchantment and her fate,
transformed from high-born lady to peasant girl;
and, moved to pity, I first searched the pages
of countless volumes of my devilish art,
and then, sealing my spirit inside
this grim and ghastly skeleton, I have come here
to reveal where the proper remedy lies
to bring relief in so pitiful a case.
O you, glory and pride of all who wear
the adamantine steel! O shining light,
O beacon, polestar, path, and guide of all
who scorn sleep and the lazy featherbed
to take up the toilsome life of blood-stained arms!
To you, great hero beyond all praise,
La Mancha's splendor and Iberia's star,
Don Quixote, as wise as you are brave — to you I say:
for the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso
to recover her original form and beauty,
your squire Sancho must lay
three thousand three hundred lashes
on his own sturdy buttocks, bared to the heavens,
and they must smart and sting and hurt him well.
So those who authored her misfortune have decreed,
and that, ladies and gentlemen, is why I have come.
after:
I am Merlin, of whom the histories
say that the devil was my father
(a lie given authority by time),
prince and monarch of magic,
and storehouse of Zoroastrian learning,
rival of the ages and the centuries
that try to bury the exploits
of brave knights-errant,
whom I have loved and still hold dear.
Although enchanters,
wizards and magicians always have
a hard, harsh, unyielding nature,
mine is tender, gentle and loving,
and eager to do good to everyone.
In the gloomy caverns of Dis,
where my soul was occupied
in drawing certain magic figures and signs,
there came the sorrowful cry of the beautiful,
peerless Dulcinea del Toboso.
I learned of her enchantment and misfortune,
and her transformation from a noble lady
into a rustic peasant girl. I pitied her,
and, enclosing my spirit in the hollow
of this frightening, fierce skeleton,
after searching a hundred thousand books
of this devilish, shameful science of mine,
I come to bring the proper remedy
for such great suffering, such great harm.
O you, glory and honour of all who wear
tunics of steel and adamant,
light and lantern, path, polestar and guide
of those who leave sluggish sleep
and idle featherbeds behind
to undertake the intolerable labour
of bloody, heavy arms!
I speak to you, O man who can never
be praised as he deserves! To you, brave
and wise Don Quixote,
splendour of La Mancha, star of Spain:
for the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso
to recover her former state,
it is necessary that Sancho, your squire,
give himself three thousand and three hundred lashes
on both his sturdy buttocks,
exposed to the air, and in such a way
that they sting, smart and torment him.
So all those responsible
for her misfortune have decreed,
and that is why I have come, my lords.
reason: Restore all 49 Spanish lines and precise images, hundred-thousand count, epochs rather than present age, Spain rather than Iberia.

before: And now daylight came, and the sun smote Sancho on the eyes with his beams. He woke, roused himself, shook himself, and stretched his lazy limbs, and seeing the havoc the pigs had made of his stores, he cursed the drove, and more besides. Then the pair resumed their journey, and as evening closed in they saw coming towards them some ten men on horseback and four or five on foot. Don Quixote's heart beat quick and Sancho's quailed with fear, for the men approaching them carried lances and shields, and were got up in very warlike fashion. Don Quixote turned to Sancho and said, "If I could use my weapons, and my promise had not tied my hands, I'd count this host coming against us as cakes and fancy bread; but perhaps it may turn out to be something other than what we fear." The men on horseback now came up, and raising their lances surrounded Don Quixote in silence, and pointed them at his back and breast, threatening him with death. One of those on foot, putting his finger to his lips as a signal for silence, seized Rocinante's bridle and drew him out of the road, and the others drove Sancho and Dapple before them, all maintaining a strange silence, and followed in the steps of the one who led Don Quixote. Don Quixote two or three times tried to ask where they were taking him and what they wanted, but the instant he began to open his lips they threatened to close them with the points of their lances; and Sancho fared the same way, for the moment he seemed about to speak one of those on foot punched him with a goad, and Dapple likewise, as if he too wanted to talk. Night set in, they quickened their pace, and the fears of the two prisoners grew greater, especially as they heard themselves assailed with — "Get on, you Troglodytes;" "Silence, you barbarians;" "March, you cannibals;" "No murmuring, you Scythians;" "Don't open your eyes, you murderous Polyphemes, you bloodthirsty lions," and other names of the kind with which their captors harassed the ears of the wretched master and man. after: And now daylight came, and the sun smote Sancho on the eyes with his beams. He woke, roused himself, shook himself, and stretched his lazy limbs, and seeing the havoc the pigs had made of his stores, he cursed the drove, and more besides. Then the pair resumed their journey, and as evening closed in they saw coming towards them some ten men on horseback and four or five on foot. Don Quixote's heart beat quick and Sancho's quailed with fear, for the men approaching them carried lances and shields, and were got up in very warlike fashion. Don Quixote turned to Sancho and said, "If I could use my weapons, and my promise had not tied my hands, I'd count this host coming against us as cakes and fancy bread; but perhaps it may turn out to be something other than what we fear." The men on horseback now came up, and raising their lances surrounded Don Quixote in silence, and pointed them at his back and breast, threatening him with death. One of those on foot, putting his finger to his lips as a signal for silence, seized Rocinante's bridle and drew him out of the road, and the others drove Sancho and Dapple before them, all maintaining a strange silence, and followed in the steps of the one who led Don Quixote. Don Quixote two or three times tried to ask where they were taking him and what they wanted, but the instant he began to open his lips they threatened to close them with the points of their lances; and Sancho fared the same way, for the moment he seemed about to speak one of those on foot punched him with a goad, and Dapple likewise, as if he too wanted to talk. Night set in, they quickened their pace, and the fears of the two prisoners grew greater, especially as they heard themselves assailed with — "Get on, you Troglodytes;" "Silence, you barbarians;" "Pay up, you cannibals;" "No murmuring, you Scythians;" "Don't open your eyes, you murderous Polyphemes, you bloodthirsty lions," and other names of the kind with which their captors harassed the ears of the wretched master and man. Sancho went along saying to himself, "We, turtledoves? We, barbers or scouring-rags? We, little dogs to be called here, here! I don't like those names at all; 'it's in a bad wind our corn is being winnowed;' 'misfortune comes upon us all at once like sticks on a dog,' and God grant it may be no worse than them that this unlucky adventure has in store for us."
